claims.text: Conventional directional solidification produces the baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy with a two-phase lamellar microstructure having approximately 5 μm spacing.
Directional solidification at a cooling rate of approximately 10^4 K/s will refine the lamellar spacing from approximately 5 μm to approximately 500 nm.
The intervention introduces no additional alloying elements.
Reducing the lamellar spacing increases the density of phase boundaries.
The increased number of phase boundaries impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances alloy strength.
The refined architecture maintains phase connectivity.
Maintained phase connectivity and the refined architecture permit greater plastic deformation.
Greater plastic deformation produced by the refined architecture increases ductility.
High-cooling-rate samples will have higher yield strength and/or ultimate tensile strength than conventionally directionally solidified samples.
High-cooling-rate samples will have greater elongation than conventionally directionally solidified samples.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvement is expected under room-temperature mechanical loading typical of structural applications.
The effect may differ at extreme temperatures or when additional alloying elements are present.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
